titre: The Name “Impressionists” Was Born of Mockery, Not Choice
accroche: A critic who wanted to ridicule a group of painters in 1874 unintentionally gave them the name they will bear forever.
contenu_vulgarise:
From April 15 to May 15, 1874, thirty painters and sculptors rejected or kept at arm's length by the official Salon show 165 works in the former studio of the photographer Nadar, on the second floor of a building on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris. The exhibition has no name. Admission costs one franc, the catalog fifty centimes, and it draws about 3,500 visitors in a month, compared with nearly 400,000 for the official Salon that same year.

## The Mechanism

On April 25, the critic Louis Leroy publishes in the satirical newspaper Le Charivari an article titled “L'exposition des impressionnistes” (The Exhibition of the Impressionists), in the form of a dialogue between himself and a fictional academic painter, Père Vincent. The latter stops in front of number 98 in the catalog, *Impression, soleil levant* (*Impression, Sunrise*), by Claude Monet, and exclaims, dismayed, that a tapestry in its early stages would be more finished than this seascape. From this word, “impression,” Leroy draws a mocking nickname for the whole group: the Impressionists. The article ridicules the canvases' unfinished handling, their colors laid on in visible touches, their refusal of the clean outline taught at the École des Beaux-Arts.

## What It Shifts

The most widespread account is right on this specific point: it is indeed Leroy who invents the word, in a mocking stroke, from Monet's painting. Before the article, the group has no fixed name: it had carried several, all given by others: “realists” or “naturalists” in the continuity of Courbet, “Batignolles school” after the café where its circle met, “Actualists,” coined by Émile Zola for Bazille, Renoir and Monet. None stuck. Leroy's did.

The real shift lies in what the painters then made of it. Rather than reject a label born to ridicule them, they adopt it themselves two years later, in 1876, at their second joint exhibition at the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel's: the mocking name becomes a banner proudly claimed. Art history today treats “Impressionism” as the natural designation of a style, when no one chose that word at a time when the style already existed: it first served to mock it, before those it targeted decided to make it their name.

This reversal is not isolated in the history of art: a nickname thrown out to disqualify a new form often ends up becoming its most convenient label, once the mockery has lost its edge and all that remains of the word is its ability to quickly designate what no one had yet named.

repere.texte: The 1874 exhibition draws about 3,500 visitors in a month, compared with nearly 400,000 for the official Salon that same year. The painters themselves adopt the name “Impressionists” in 1876, at their second exhibition.

carte.punch: The name “Impressionists” was born of a mockery published in a satirical newspaper in 1874.
carte.idee: The critic Louis Leroy coins the mocking nickname “Impressionists” in 1874, from a Monet painting, when the group still had no fixed name. Two years later, the painters themselves adopt it as the name of their movement.

quiz.question: What does the history of the word “Impressionist” really show, beyond Louis Leroy's mockery?
choix: That the word was already circulating in the group's discussions before Leroy's article, which only made it public and mocking
That they rejected this mocking nickname until the end of the 19th century
That they themselves adopted, in 1876, the nickname Leroy had invented two years earlier to mock them
That the official Salon itself invented this name to sideline the rejected artists
quiz.explication: The word is indeed invented by Leroy in 1874; before him, the group had no fixed name (“realists,” “Batignolles school,” “Actualists,” depending on who was speaking). Rather than reject this mocking nickname, the painters adopt it themselves in 1876, at their second exhibition.
